hints: Think what a voltmeter reading actually measures when two different half cells are joined together.
walkthrough:
Picture what $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ means**
Think of two separate half cells joined up. Electrons want to flow from the more easily oxidised side to the more easily reduced side. The voltage you measure for that push is the cell potential. The word standard just means you measure it when everything is in its standard state so values can be compared fairly.

Final answer: The e.m.f. of a cell formed from two half cells under standard conditions, with ion concentrations of $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, temperature of $298 \text{ K}$ and any gases at $1 \text{ atm}$.

hints: Think what two connections are needed between the beakers, one for electrons to be measured and one for ions to complete the circuit.
walkthrough:
Complete the circuit in two places**
You already have two beakers with electrode and solution in each. For a cell to work you need electrons to travel round the outside and ions to travel on the inside. So join the two metal electrodes with a wire through a voltmeter, this measures the potential without drawing current. Then dip a salt bridge containing e.g. $\text{KNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$ between the two solutions to allow ion flow and maintain electrical neutrality.
Final answer: Connect the two electrodes with a voltmeter (via wires) and connect the two solutions with a salt bridge.

hints: Decide which half cell contains only one metal and its ion, so the solid can act as its own electrode.
Decide which half cell contains two ions of the same element in different oxidation states, so it needs an inert conductor.
Recall which metal is used as the inert electrode and that both ions must be present together at $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the simple metal ion system**
The $\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}$ system has a solid metal in equilibrium with its own ion: $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$. That means the silver rod itself conducts electrons in and out. So A is the $\text{Ag}$ electrode sitting in B which is $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$.

Spot the system with no solid metal**
The $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ system is $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$. Both forms are in solution, so there is nothing to carry electrons to the wire. You must add an inert conductor that does not react. That is platinum. So C is $\text{Pt}$ and D is a mixture of $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$.

Remember standard concentrations**
Because this is measurement of $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$, every ion must be at $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. So B is $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and D contains $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ plus $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. The left and right beakers can be swapped, as long as electrode matches its solution.

Final answer: A = $\text{Ag(s)}$
B = $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$, $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
C = $\text{Pt(s)}$
D = $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$, both $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: Compare $E^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}) = +0.80 \text{ V}$ with $E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77 \text{ V}$ to decide which ion is the stronger oxidant.
walkthrough:
Let the stronger oxidant win**
Look up the values: $E^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}) = +0.80 \text{ V}$ is more positive than $E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77 \text{ V}$. More positive means a greater tendency to gain electrons and be reduced. So $\text{Ag}^{+}$ will take an electron from $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is reduced to $\text{Ag}$ while $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is oxidised to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, giving $$\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \longrightarrow \text{Ag(s)} + \text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$$

hints: Substitute $[\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.31 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ into $E = E^{\ominus} + 0.059\log[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ and think whether log of a number less than 1 is negative.
Remember $E_{cell} = E_{positive} - E_{negative}$, here $E(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag})$ minus $E(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+})$ which stays at $+0.77 \text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Correct the silver potential for dilution**
Lowering $[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ shifts $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$ to the left, making reduction less favourable, so $E$ falls below $E^{\ominus}$. Put the numbers in: $$E = E^{\ominus} + 0.059\log[\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})]$$ $$E = 0.80 + 0.059\log(0.31)$$ $\log(0.31) = -0.51$, so $0.059 \times -0.51 = -0.03$. Hence $$E = 0.80 - 0.03 = +0.77 \text{ V}$$

Combine with the unchanged iron half cell**
The iron half cell is still standard, so $E(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77 \text{ V}$. Cell e.m.f. is positive minus negative: $$E_{cell} = E(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}) - E(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+})$$ $$E_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.77 = 0.0 \text{ V}$$ At this concentration the two half cells have equal potential, so there is no driving force.
